To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the prevalence of RA is increasing; (ii) the prevalence of obesity is increasing; (iii) RA patients have a higher prevalence of obesity than the general population; (iv) RA patients have higher levels of body fat, lower levels of muscle mass, and lower levels of bone mineral density than the general population.
the presence of early RA is associated with an increase in body mass, and that this is related to an increase in fat mass and a decrease in lean mass, particularly in the legs.
early RA is associated with loss of muscle and fat mass, but the magnitude and direction of the changes are dependent on the type of RA medication used.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of RA on body composition.
understanding the mechanisms that underlie the relationship between obesity, inflammation and the risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis.

understanding the mechanisms that underlie the development of osteoporosis and sarcopenia in rheumatoid arthritis, and the role of these mechanisms in the development of frailty and functional impairment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no conclusive evidence that rheumatoid arthritis is associated with an increased prevalence of obesity.
there is no evidence to support a link between the consumption of dietary fat and the development of rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
the evidence is inconclusive regarding the effect of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) on the development and progression of osteoporosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the body composition of patients with RA is altered and that this alteration may have an impact on disease activity.

the early rheumatoid arthritis patients have a higher fat mass and lower muscle mass compared to healthy controls, and that this difference in body composition may be associated with a higher risk of disability and mortality in RA patients.
the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis is multifactorial.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the early stages of rheumatoid arthritis are associated with changes in body composition, and these changes are not explained by the presence of disease-related inflammation or the use of glucocorticoids or disease modifying anti-rheumatic drugs.
we have shown for the first time that there is an association between the presence of early rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and changes in body composition.
the body composition in patients with rheumatoid arthritis is altered, with a reduction in lean muscle and an increase in adipose tissue, especially visceral adipose tissue.
